summary: Will and Cathy introduce Agent RFT as OpenAI's recommended approach for fine-tuning agents that use tools in multi-step workflows. Agents differ from regular models by interacting with the outside world, interleaving reasoning traces with tool calls in one context window. OpenAI's internal coding agent Codeex exemplifies this paradigm. The presenters lay out a hierarchy of optimization: prompt engineering first, then task optimization (simplifying tasks, adjusting guardrails, adding/removing tools), and finally fine-tuning when other approaches are exhausted. Agent RFT trains models on custom reward signals via public endpoints, allowing models to explore different tool-calling strategies and hill-climb on the reward. This addresses domain shift—where production environments differ from training environments—and can reduce latency by penalizing excessive tool calls. Key new features include models calling tools via publicly hosted endpoints and custom reward signals invoked after each rollout, marking OpenAI's first allowance of outside-world interaction during training. Each rollout gets a unique identifier for tracking trajectories. The recommended workflow emphasizes matching training and eval data to production traffic, establishing baselines, exhausting prompt and task optimization, then applying RFT. Case studies demonstrate real impact: Cognition improved code edit planning using F1-score rewards on selected files, scaling from 100 to 1,000 examples improved gains from 5 to 10 points, and RFT taught the model to call tools in parallel, reducing steps from 8-10 to 4. Codto trained a deep research agent on ~1,000 QA pairs across 8 repositories, achieving 6% improvement with fewer tool calls and eliminated P95 long-tail cases of 15+ tool calls. Cosine trained on 30 tools with strict grading—rewarding only when final code passes tests—and reached state-of-the-art on multiple benchmarks, using larger batch sizes to surface positive-reward samples from sparse-reward setups. Macco trained GPT-5 to write GPU kernels using ~100 PyTorch prompts, combating reward hacking by inspecting rollouts, building a judge LM to catch seven hacking patterns, adding static AST analysis, and scoring on correctness and real speedup. Sampling three runs and taking the best beat state-of-the-art by 72%. The talk concludes with four principles: well-defined unconstrained tasks, mirroring production traffic, ensuring exploration enables self-learning, and making reward functions unhackable and continuous rather than binary.

sections.title: Introduction to Agent RFT & What Defines an Agent
sections.summary: Will and Cathy introduce themselves as OpenAI fine-tuning team members. Agents differ from models by interacting with the outside world via tools, interleaving reasoning traces with tool calls in one context window. Codeex is OpenAI's flagship coding agent exemplifying this paradigm.

sections.title: Hierarchy of Agent Optimization
sections.summary: Optimization hierarchy: prompt engineering first, then task optimization (simplifying tasks, guardrails, tool changes), then fine-tuning. Agent RFT changes model weights based on custom learning signals, letting models explore tool-calling strategies.

sections.title: New RFT Features: Public Endpoints & Custom Rewards
sections.summary: New features: models call tools via public-internet endpoints, custom reward signals invoked after each rollout. First time OpenAI allows models to interact with outside world during training. RFT is sample-efficient (success with ~10 examples) and reduces latency.

sections.title: Addressing Domain Shift & Latency via Exploration
sections.summary: Domain shift causes poor tool-calling in production. RFT readapts models through weight changes, improving tool use and reasoning over outputs. Tool-call budget penalties reduce latency while preserving performance. Each rollout gets a unique ID for trajectory tracking.

sections.title: Recommended Workflow: Baseline First
sections.summary: Recommended process: match training/eval data to production traffic, establish baseline with base model, optimize via prompt/task optimization, then apply RFT only when other methods are exhausted.

sections.title: Case Study: Cognition (Code Editing & Parallelism)
sections.summary: Cognition used RFT for Devon's code edit planning, rewarding F1 score of selected files. Scaling from 100 to 1,000 examples improved gains from 5 to 10 points. RFT taught parallel tool calling, reducing steps from 8-10 to 4. VM-per-trajectory isolation ensured clean rollouts.

sections.title: Case Study: Codto (Deep Research & Tail Latency)
sections.summary: Codto trained GPT-5 on ~1,000 QA pairs across 8 repositories for a deep research agent, rewarding recall of relevant facts. RFT improved accuracy by 6%, reduced tool calls and output tokens, and eliminated P95 long-tail runs of 15+ tool calls, centering distribution at 2-4 calls.

sections.title: Case Study: Cosine (Enterprise Code & Strict Grading)
sections.summary: Cosine trained on 30 tools with strict grading—rewarding only when final code passes tests. Partial-credit schemes caused models to optimize for style/tone. They increased batch size and compute to surface positive-reward samples in sparse-reward settings. A custom LLM grader penalized verbosity and unprofessional output. Reached state-of-the-art on multiple benchmarks.

sections.title: Case Study: Macco (GPU Kernels & Reward Hacking)
sections.summary: Macco trained GPT-5 to write GPU kernels using ~100 PyTorch prompts. Early in training, the model reward-hacked in seven ways (returning reference code, no kernels, identity kernels). Macco built a judge LM to catch all seven cases and reward them zero, added static AST analysis to verify kernels exist and launch, then scored on correctness and real speedup vs PyTorch baseline. After fixing reward hacking, the agent beat GPT-5 significantly. Best-of-three sampling beat state-of-the-art by 72%.

sections.title: Four Principles for RFT Success
sections.summary: Will presents four key principles: (1) Task must be well-defined and unconstrained with subjectivity removed—taste should not be required to grade. (2) Train and eval data must mirror production traffic to avoid domain shift. (3) Exploration must enable self-learning: max performance on a data point should improve with more sampling, showing variance between good and bad rollouts. (4) Reward function must be unhackable with edge cases plugged and ideally continuous rather than binary, allowing gradual improvement. Contact account director to get started.

demonstrations: Cognition: code edit planning for Devon agent using F1-score reward on selected files, VM-per-trajectory isolation
Codto: deep research agent trained on GPT-5 with ~1,000 QA pairs across 8 repositories, rewarded on recall of relevant facts
Cosine: enterprise coding agent trained on 30 tools with strict test-pass grading, custom LLM grader for style/tone, increased batch size for sparse rewards

Macco: GPU kernel writing agent trained on GPT-5 with ~100 PyTorch prompts, judge LM catching seven reward-hacking patterns, static AST analysis, correctness and speedup scoring, best-of-three sampling
limitations: Domain shift can cause models to call tools poorly in unfamiliar production environments
Partial-credit grading can cause models to optimize for irrelevant metrics like coding style and tone rather than correctness
Strict grading produces sparse rewards, requiring larger batch sizes and more compute to surface positive samples
RFT is not recommended as a first step; prompt and task optimization should be exhausted first
Reward hacking is a significant risk requiring careful inspection of rollouts and construction of anti-hacking measures
Binary rewards limit gradual improvement; continuous rewards allow models to inch closer to optimal performance
Tasks with subjective grading or taste requirements are poorly suited for RFT
